snip.t: Haemorrhagic stroke – sudden neurological deficit caused by intracerebral bleeding (parenchymal haemorrhage) or subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) from rupture of a vessel.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the subarachnoid space (between the pia and arachnoid membranes).
| Subarachnoid haemorrhage | Thunderclap headache, sudden collapse, no prodrome | Xanthochromia, bloody CSF, no fever initially |
Subarachnoid haemorrhage: bleeding into the subarachnoid space; classically presents with a sudden, severe headache.
| Subarachnoid haemorrhage | Thunderclap headache, neck stiffness, photophobia | CT shows sulcal blood; lumbar puncture shows xanthochromia if CT negative. |
Vascular: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, hypertensive encephalopathy, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — Uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy, dehydration
Subarachnoid haemorrhage → blood in CSF → meningeal irritation + sudden rise in ICP → thunderclap headache

qs.q: A 60-year-old patient who suffered a sudden thunderclap headache undergoes a lumbar puncture 12 hours after symptom onset. Which specific cerebrospinal fluid finding confirms the diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage?
o: Decreased opening pressure with high protein
Xanthochromia due to bilirubin in the supernatant
Clear fluid with isolated lymphocytic pleocytosis
Presence of neutrophils and low glucose
qs.e: Xanthochromia, caused by the presence of bilirubin in the supernatant after centrifugation of CSF, confirms true subarachnoid haemorrhage rather than a traumatic lumbar puncture. Neutrophils and low glucose are characteristic of bacterial meningitis.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man is admitted following a spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage. He is stuporous and exhibits dense right-sided hemiparesis. Using the Hunt and Hess scale, how should this patient be graded?
o: Grade 5
Grade 2
Grade 3
Grade 4
qs.e: Hunt and Hess Grade 4 is defined by stupor and hemiparesis. Grade 5 represents a comatose patient with decerebrate posturing.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man is admitted with a severe spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage. Which of the following systemic complications or associated findings is frequently monitored during the acute laboratory and diagnostic workup?
o: Respiratory alkalosis caused by primary hyperventilation
Hypernatremia resulting from diabetes insipidus
Hyponatremia with nonspecific ECG abnormalities, e.g., prolonged QT interval
Thrombocytosis accompanied by increased fibrinogen concentration
qs.e: Patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage frequently develop hyponatraemia and characteristic cardiac abnormalities, including non-specific ST and T wave changes, prolonged QT intervals, U waves, and arrhythmias. Diabetes insipidus typically causes hypernatraemia, which is less common than hyponatraemia in this context.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman is admitted with a Hunt and Hess grade 4 subarachnoid haemorrhage and becomes progressively drowsy and stuporous within the first 18 hours of admission. A repeat CT scan shows acute ventricular enlargement. What is the most appropriate acute intervention?
o: Start oral nimodipine therapy for 21 days
Insert an external ventricular drain
Place a permanent ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Apply a titanium surgical clip through craniotomy
qs.e: Acute hydrocephalus occurring within 24 hours presents with drowsiness or coma and is treated with an external ventricular drain. Chronic communicating hydrocephalus is treated with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man develops hyponatraemia on day 6 after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Investigations reveal high urinary sodium excretion and euvolaemia clinically, pointing towards cerebral salt wasting. What is the most appropriate management approach?
o: Emergency insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Stop all intravenous crystalloid fluid administration
Give isotonic or hypertonic saline solution
Immediately restrict daily free‑water intake
qs.e: Hyponatraemia due to cerebral salt wasting or SIADH is treated with isotonic or hypertonic saline, and fluid restriction must be avoided because it worsens cerebral vasospasm. Fludrocortisone can also be used.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 44-year-old man is admitted with a severe thunderclap headache. A lumbar puncture confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage. During the first 48 hours, he develops frequent premature ventricular complexes and bradycardia. What is the most important initial laboratory parameter to check and correct?
o: Check and correct serum creatinine levels
Check and correct serum potassium levels
Check and correct blood glucose levels
Check and correct serum calcium levels
qs.e: Cardiac arrhythmias occur in up to 90 percent of patients, usually in the first 48 hours, and checking and correcting potassium is an essential step in management. Neurogenic stunned myocardium and ECG changes can also mimic acute coronary syndromes.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 56-year-old man who suffered a subarachnoid haemorrhage develops severe respiratory distress and frothy sputum on day 3. Chest radiography reveals bilateral infiltrates in the absence of left atrial hypertension. Which therapy is most appropriate for this neurogenic complication?
o: Continuous infusion of short-acting nitrates to reduce afterload
Immediate aggressive fluid loading to maintain high central venous pressure
Prophylactic broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Diuresis, dobutamine, and positive end-expiratory pressure
qs.e: Neurogenic pulmonary oedema is almost universal in severe subarachnoid haemorrhage and is managed with diuresis, dobutamine, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). Nitrates should be avoided because they raise intracranial pressure.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 61-year-old woman is admitted with a Hunt and Hess grade 2 subarachnoid haemorrhage. While monitoring her intracranial pressure and cerebral perfusion, osmotic agents are required. Which of the following agents is specifically indicated for raised intracranial pressure in this setting?
o: Mannitol
Furosemide
Hydrochlorothiazide
Spironolactone
qs.e: Mannitol or hypertonic saline are osmotic agents used alongside head elevation and brief hyperventilation to manage raised intracranial pressure. Loop diuretics like furosemide are not standard primary osmotic agents for acute intracranial pressure crises.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

es.q: List and explain the main causes and risk factors associated with spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage.
es.m:
- **Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm:** Accounts for approximately 75% to 85% of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage cases.
- **Arteriovenous malformation (AVM):** Represents about 10% of cases and serves as the second commonest identifiable cause.
- **Other rare causes:** Includes perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal haemorrhage, arterial dissection, mycotic aneurysms from infective endocarditis, tumours, coagulopathies, anticoagulants, cocaine use, sickle cell disease, and cerebral venous thrombosis.
- **Demographic and lifestyle risk factors:** Hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol use, female sex, and an average age around 50 years.
- **Associated medical conditions:** Autosomal dominant

es.q: Discuss the classic clinical presentation and warning leaks of an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
es.m:
- **Thunderclap headache:** Sudden, severe headache described as "the worst headache of my life", reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute, often occurring during exertion.
- **Associated symptoms:** Nausea and vomiting, photophobia, visual changes, back and bilateral leg pain.
- **Meningeal signs:** Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) and a positive Kernig's sign, which take several hours to develop.
- **Systemic and neurological manifestations:** Loss of consciousness at ictus in up to 45% of patients, acute phase seizures, and focal neurological signs such as hemiparesis or cranial nerve palsies.

es.q: Outline the diagnostic investigation pathway for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage.
es.m:
- **Non-contrast CT head:** Performed within 6 hours of onset for near 100% sensitivity; demonstrates blood in basal cisterns and subarachnoid spaces, intraventricular blood, or hydrocephalus.
- **Lumbar puncture:** Indicated if CT is negative despite high suspicion; reveals xanthochromia (bilirubin in supernatant) and a persistently high red cell count across all tubes.
- **Angiography:** Computed tomography angiography (CTA) or digital subtraction cerebral angiography (the gold standard) is used to delineate the aneurysm site, size, shape, and neck.
- **Auxiliary blood tests:** Full blood count, coagulation profile, cross-match, electrolytes (checking for hyponatraemia), and glucose levels

es.q: Discuss in detail the pathophysiology, clinical grading, immediate medical stabilisation, and management of complications associated with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
es.m:
- **Pathological anatomy of aneurysms:** Saccular berry aneurysms arise at branching sites of large circle of Willis arteries due to haemodynamic stress and defects in the tunica media and internal elastic lamina, with about 85% occurring in the anterior circulation.
- **Rupture distribution sites:** Internal carotid artery including the posterior communicating junction accounts for about 41%, anterior communicating/anterior cerebral artery for about 34%, middle cerebral artery for about 20%, and the vertebrobasilar system for about 4%.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the space between the arachnoid and pia mater, most often from a ruptured aneurysm. It presents with a sudden, severe headache and can rapidly cause neurological decline. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent death or permanent disability.

sections.p: SAH is the presence of blood in the subarachnoid space, confirmed by imaging or lumbar puncture. The classic presentation is a thunderclap headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.
b: Diagnosed by non‑contrast CT within 6 h (sensitivity ≈ 95 %)
If CT negative, perform lumbar puncture for xanthochromia

t.b: Positive → SAH confirmed; negative after 6 h requires LP
Xanthochromia → SAH confirmed; clear fluid → SAH unlikely

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Hunt‑Hess scale (clinical) and the Fisher scale (radiologic). Higher grades predict poorer outcome and guide intensity of care.
b: Hunt‑Hess I‑IV: assess consciousness, focal deficits, and meningismus
Fisher 1‑4: amount of blood on CT

sections.p: Most SAH originates from a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm; other causes are less common but important in low‑resource settings.
b: Infective causes: mycotic aneurysm (e.g., HIV, TB)

sections.p: Patients describe a sudden, maximal intensity headache (“worst of life”), often with nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and sometimes loss of consciousness.
Imaging and CSF analysis confirm SAH and identify the source. When advanced imaging is unavailable, bedside ultrasound and clinical clues guide management.

t.b: Aneurysm identified → plan endovascular or surgical repair; none → consider other sources
Confirms lesion for definitive treatment; if unavailable, CTA is acceptable
Positive → SAH confirmed; negative does not rule out early bleed

sections.p: Early complications can be fatal; vigilance for these signs directs urgent intervention.
Initial care stabilises airway, breathing, circulation, and prevents rebleeding. Definitive treatment targets the bleeding source and mitigates complications.
b: Control blood pressure (target < 140 mmHg systolic) without causing hypoperfusion
Early aneurysm securing: endovascular coiling or surgical clipping
Treat hydrocephalus with external ventricular drain
Manage seizures with levetiracetam if clinically indicated

sections.p: After securing the lesion, monitor for delayed vasospasm and hydrocephalus, and address modifiable risk factors.
b: Transcranial Doppler to screen for vasospasm
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, blood pressure control

sections.p: Conditions that mimic SAH share headache and meningeal irritation but differ in management.
b: Intracerebral haemorrhage extending into subarachnoid space

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming, especially when resources are limited.
b: CT performed > 6 h may miss small bleed → rely on LP

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache, loss of consciousness, new neurological deficit, vomiting, or seizures require immediate emergency care

faq.q: Why is a thunderclap headache considered SAH until proven otherwise?
faq.a: Because the probability of SAH is high and missing it can be fatal; early imaging is mandatory.

faq.q: What is the role of nimodipine in SAH?
faq.a: It is a calcium‑channel blocker that reduces the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm.

faq.q: When is lumbar puncture indicated if CT is negative?
faq.a: When the CT is done after the first 6 hours or when clinical suspicion remains high despite a normal scan.
